implementation_notes: Jakarta Persistence states this pattern verbatim: JOINED means a table for each abstract or concrete entity class, containing only the columns mapped to fields the class declares, with a join used to retrieve an instance's state. Annotate the root with @Entity @Inheritance(strategy = JOINED) and a @DiscriminatorColumn, let the shared @Id be the join key, and the provider generates the joins; em.find(Party.class, id) returns concrete subtypes polymorphically. Hand-written SQL stays justified for bulk and reporting paths, where materialising the entity graph is pure overhead.
pitfalls: The discriminator column belongs to the root table and polymorphic queries need it; without it a Party query returns only rows that cannot be resolved to a subtype.
Subclass attributes that are lazy-loaded throw LazyInitializationException on a detached entity; fetch the path eagerly or with an entity graph when the subclass data is needed.

variants.name: Hand-written JDBC mapper (PreparedStatement / transaction)
variants.idiom_name: PreparedStatement per path inside one JDBC transaction
variants.implementation_notes: Without a provider you own the mapping: one PreparedStatement per path, ResultSet to object conversion, and a single JDBC transaction (setAutoCommit(false) plus commit/rollback) so all tables of the path change together - RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS supplies the shared key the subtype insert reuses. Reads either join the full path for a concrete type or fetch the base row and its type code and dispatch in Java. This form is justified for batch jobs, legacy schemas and reporting queries, where a persistence context would be dead weight.
pitfalls: Leaving auto-commit on splits the two inserts into separate transactions and can leave a base row without its subtype row.
SELECT * across a join returns duplicate column names; alias columns or read by index, otherwise the wrong value lands in the wrong field.
